title: Concurrent rendering
description: Understand how concurrent rendering lets React prepare multiple UI states at once without blocking user input or animations.

data.text: Concurrent rendering is a behind-the-scenes mode that lets React prepare new UIs in the background while the current UI stays interactive. Instead of blocking the main thread until a large update finishes, React can pause, resume, and even abandon work based on what the user is doing.

Concurrent mode is not a separate API you turn on globally. It is a set of behaviors triggered by specific primitives: `useTransition`, `useDeferredValue`, and `<Suspense>`. When you use these, React may render the same component multiple times before showing the result, keeping the app responsive throughout.

items: Render work can be split across multiple frames
React may render a component more than once before committing
User input and animations continue during heavy renders
Only the final committed state is visible to the user

cards.title: Legacy rendering
cards.description: The default behavior before React 18. Updates block the main thread until completion.

cards.title: Concurrent rendering
cards.description: React 18+ default for features like transitions and Suspense. Updates are interruptible.

data.title: Deferring expensive filtering
data.content: useDeferredValue lets a text input stay snappy while a heavy list filters in the background.

items: Concurrent mode is not on by default for every setState — only for transition-like APIs
Concurrent rendering does not make code run faster; it keeps the UI responsive
Effects still run once per commit; concurrency does not change effect semantics

data.title: Concurrency is about responsiveness, not raw speed
data.text: React may render the same tree twice before committing. This is intentional. The goal is to let the browser paint user input immediately, not to minimize the number of renders.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Concurrent rendering splits work across frames instead of blocking
Transitions and deferred values opt specific updates into concurrency
The UI stays responsive even when React is processing large trees
data.takeaway: If your app feels sluggish during filtering, sorting, or tab switches, wrap the heavy work in a transition instead of micro-optimizing individual components.
